design_detail: Cross-sectional PET study (Brain 2010;133:1779-1797) of serotonin transporter binding with [11C]DASB in 49 people who used ecstasy and 50 people who did not, recruited by advertisement in Toronto, with scalp-hair toxicology to confirm ecstasy use and detect other stimulants. Binding potential (BPND) was estimated with the Logan graphical method using cerebellar cortex as reference, in 13 regions, with partial-volume correction, two further kinetic models, manual as well as automatic region drawing, and a whole-brain voxel-wise analysis. Structural MRI (volumes and cortical thickness), a battery of cognitive tests, mood scales, blood hormones and serotonin-transporter promoter genotyping were collected in the same people.
can_establish: That in this sample, with ecstasy use confirmed in hair, transporter binding was lower in every cerebral cortical region and in the hippocampus, that it was unchanged in striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus and midbrain, that the cortical reduction was not explained by brain volume, cortical thickness, hormones, genotype, sex or hair-confirmed use of methamphetamine, cocaine or cannabis, and that lower binding went with more years of use and a higher maximum dose.
cannot_establish: That ecstasy caused the reduction (one scan per person, no pre-use measurement); that the reduction means loss of serotonin terminals rather than lower transporter expression; that the cognitive differences are caused by it (correlational, uncorrected); or anything about recovery, since abstinence was typically only 1-2 months and showed no relation with binding.

sample.recruitment: Advertisements in the Toronto area; full assessment interview with SCID for DSM-IV, health questionnaire, brief neurological examination, mood and sleep questionnaires, drug-history questionnaire, urine screens at each visit and before the scan, and a scalp-hair drug screen (pp. 1781-1782).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Both groups: 18-40 years, no psychotropic medication, no first-degree family history of DSM-IV Axis I disorder, no medical illness or brain trauma that could affect the serotonin system. Comparison group: no illicit drug use on hair or urine testing except cannabis. Ecstasy group: hair positive for ecstasy plus self-report; an Axis I condition was an exclusion only if it began before ecstasy use (p. 1781).
sample.demographics: Ecstasy group 28 men, 21 women, mean age 25.9 (SEM 0.8); comparison group 25 men, 25 women, 26.0 (0.9), p=0.90. The ecstasy group had fewer years of education (14.6 vs 16.0, p=0.002), lower premorbid IQ (107.4 vs 111.6, p=0.002) and slightly lower body mass index (23.4 vs 24.7, p=0.04); 30 vs 5 were current smokers and 25 vs 1 used cannabis at least monthly (both p<0.0001) (Table 1, p. 1784).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single session). Scans of three participants were corrected for head movement; some cognitive and hormone data are missing for a few people (Ns given per test in Table 4).
sample.selection_effects: Volunteers for a study of ecstasy, with a comparison group screened to be free of illicit drugs other than cannabis; the ecstasy group was therefore also a group with much heavier tobacco, cannabis and stimulant use. The authors describe the sample as typical low-to-moderate ecstasy use (median 1.5 tablets per session, about 2 sessions a month, median 126 lifetime tablets).

exposure.measurement: Self-report questionnaire plus scalp-hair analysis for ecstasy, MDA, methamphetamine, amphetamine, cocaine and opioids (hair grows about 0.5 inch a month, so it covers roughly 5 months in men and about 21 months in women in this sample), urine screens at interviews and before the scan (pp. 1781, 1784).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: All oral except one person who used crushed tablets intranasally. Mean 4.1 years of use (range 0.5-12); 206 (SEM 31) lifetime tablets, median 126, range 4-922; typical monthly dose median 2.3 tablets; dose per session median 1.5 tablets (80% typically 1-2); maximum dose per session median 3, range 1-20 (Table 2, p. 1785).
exposure.polysubstance: Hair confirmed MDMA in all 49; MDA in 40 (82%); methamphetamine or amphetamine in 32 (65%); cocaine in 23 (47%). Only 9 of the 32 with methamphetamine-positive hair reported recent use (p=0.016). Self-reported co-use in the previous 6 months included alcohol (84%), cannabis (76%), ketamine (37%) and GHB (20%) (Table 2, p. 1785). Binding differences were analysed separately in those positive and negative for methamphetamine and cocaine in hair and were similar (p. 1787).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Reported abstinence from illicit drugs for at least 14 days; mean 45.2 days since last ecstasy (SEM 4.7; median 38, range 11-194) (Table 2, p. 1785).

comparison.controls: 50 people recruited by the same advertisements with no illicit drug use on hair and urine testing except cannabis (p. 1781).
comparison.matching: Matched on age, sex and ethnicity; not matched on education, premorbid IQ, smoking, alcohol or cannabis, which all differed.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use measurement; the paper states explicitly that a premorbid difference in transporter levels is one of the possible explanations of the finding (p. 1791).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Cannabis in 1 of 50 at least monthly, 5 of 50 current smokers; no other illicit drugs on hair or urine.

outcomes.instruments: [11C]DASB PET on a high-resolution head-dedicated camera (in-plane resolution 2.8 mm), 90-min scans; BPND by Logan graphical analysis with cerebellar cortex as reference, also SRTM2 and MRTM2; geometric transfer matrix partial-volume correction; T1 MRI for CIVET volumes and cortical thickness; cognitive battery (WASI, NART, PASAT, Digit Ordering, Trails, Symbol Digit, Consonant Trigrams, CVLT, Warrington, Denman); mood scales (IDS, HAM, SIGHD/SAD); blood oestradiol, testosterone and FSH; 5-HTTLPR genotyping (pp. 1782-1783).
outcomes.validity_norms: [11C]DASB is selective for the serotonin transporter; cerebellum is nearly free of it. Cognitive tests have published norms, and both groups' IQ scores were in the normal range (p. 1789). A binding potential is a surrogate for terminal integrity.
outcomes.operationalization: Serotonin neuron status is operationalized as regional BPND; cognitive deficit as a lower group mean on a test, tested one-tailed.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni-corrected least-significant-difference tests for the 13 regional binding comparisons, and false-discovery-rate correction in the voxel-wise and cortical-thickness analyses; Bonferroni correction for the cognitive tests, which were tested one-tailed; the correlations between binding and cognition are reported uncorrected (pp. 1783, 1786, 1790).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Manual regions of interest were drawn by a research assistant blinded to group; the automatic segmentation is group-blind by construction (p. 1782).

analysis.effect_sizes: Region-by-group interaction F(12,1152)=7.24, p corrected <0.0001. Reductions in the ecstasy group were confined to the cerebral cortices and hippocampus (p corrected <0.001), largest in occipital cortex (-46%); after partial-volume correction, occipital -39%, temporal -34%, hippocampus -31%, cingulate -30%, insular -27%, parietal -19%, frontal -17% (all p<0.01). No difference in caudate, putamen, ventral striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus or midbrain; the three kinetic models agreed (occipital -46%, -46%, -41%; hippocampus -21%, -21%, -15%; striatum +3%, +2%, +8%). Voxel-wise: largest cluster in occipital cortex, peak magnitude -62% (false-discovery-rate corrected p<0.0001). Effect sizes for binding: occipital 1.14, insular 1.10. In the insular cortex 51% of the ecstasy group fell below the lowest control value. Regression within the ecstasy group: only years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding, F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001; years of use also predicted lower caudate binding, F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032. No correlation between days since last use and binding. Cognition: lower scores in the ecstasy group on the CVLT (group F(1,93)=8.53, p=0.004, short-delay free recall -17.8%), PASAT, Digit Ordering, Trails B and Symbol Digit, with effect sizes 0.43-0.86, after adjustment for education or verbal IQ; no difference on Denman or Warrington memory tests. Binding in insular cortex and hippocampus correlated with CVLT short-delay free recall (rho=0.38, p=0.004) and Trails B (rho=-0.38 and -0.35).
analysis.covariates: Education and verbal IQ as covariates for the cognitive comparisons; analyses of binding repeated within subgroups defined by hair results for methamphetamine and cocaine, by self-reported cannabis, ketamine, LSD, mushrooms and tobacco, by sex, body mass index, Axis I diagnosis, hormone levels and genotype (p. 1787).
analysis.selective_reporting: Regions, models and subgroup analyses are reported in full in text and supplement; several supplementary tables (manual regions, model comparison, subgroup binding, volumes) were not read here.
analysis.power: Stated for the striatum: with this sample and a coefficient of variation of 16%, a difference as small as 8% would have been detected with 80% power (p. 1793).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Group means of cortical and hippocampal transporter binding were about a fifth to a half lower in people with hair-confirmed ecstasy use, with striatum, pallidum, thalamus and midbrain unchanged; the difference was not explained by the structural, hormonal, genetic and other-drug factors tested; individual values overlapped heavily except in insular cortex; and binding related to years of use and maximum dose but not to time since last use.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract reads the finding as a 'highly selective mild to marked loss of serotonin transporter' comparable in size to that in Parkinson's disease, and speaks of susceptibility of cortical serotonergic neurons. The Discussion is more careful, listing lower transporter concentration in intact neurons, loss of terminals and a premorbid difference as alternatives (p. 1791). The cognitive section is also careful: it notes near-total overlap with controls and that people may have drifted to a poorer-performing peer group (p. 1790).

timeline.event: First [11C]DASB study reporting the same cortical pattern in 23 people
Same group's follow-up in 16 people with the same tracer (McCann et al., Psychopharmacology 200:439-450); not read here.
Independent study with the same tracer reporting cortical, pallidostriatal and amygdala reductions and a dose relation
Independent study with arterial input confirming the cortical pattern and adding higher 5-HT2A binding
Review counting 14 of 16 human imaging studies with significantly lower transporter binding

replication.where_it_stands: This was the first independent replication of the cortical pattern reported by the Baltimore group with the same tracer, and the only large study with hair verification of exposure; the sex difference reported from SPECT (Reneman et al., 2001) was not reproduced here, where reductions were of similar size in men and women.

funding.funder: US National Institutes of Health (NIDA DA017301), Canadian Institutes of Health Research MOP-49538, Canadian Psychiatric Foundation (Funding, p. 1794).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article (searched in the text extraction of all pages).
funding.affiliations_note: Centre for Addiction and Mental Health and University of Toronto; the senior author has published critiques of the field's interpretation of transporter imaging, including in methamphetamine (Kish et al., 2017).

what_would_settle_it: Repeat scanning of the same people over years of abstinence with a selective tracer and verified exposure, together with a measure able to separate lower transporter expression from loss of terminals (for example transporter protein and other terminal markers post mortem in people with documented use, or a second serotonin terminal marker in vivo).

domains.note: The ecstasy group smoked more, used more cannabis and alcohol, had less education and lower premorbid IQ; two thirds had methamphetamine-positive hair. Subgroup analyses address these one at a time rather than adjusting jointly, and the comparison of binding is unadjusted.

Hair confirms recent exposure for all participants and detects undisclosed stimulant use, which is a strength; amounts, years and abstinence remain self-reported, and hair covers only about 5 months in men.
Self-selected volunteers; no pre-use measurement, so a premorbid difference cannot be excluded, as the paper says.
Few missing data; Ns are given per test.
Selective tracer, high-resolution camera, three kinetic models, partial-volume correction, blinded manual regions and a voxel-wise check; the outcome remains a surrogate for terminal integrity.

Regional comparisons corrected, voxel-wise analyses false-discovery-rate corrected, negative findings reported; the cognitive tests were one-tailed, and the binding-cognition correlations are uncorrected.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Technically the strongest of the imaging studies read here (largest sample, selective tracer, hair verification, several analyses that could have overturned the finding), but still a cross-sectional comparison of self-selected groups differing in education, IQ, tobacco, cannabis and stimulant use, with no pre-use measurement. It can be cited for the size and regional pattern of the group difference and for its relation to years of use and maximum dose, not for causation or for a loss of nerve terminals.

key_findings.finding: Serotonin transporter binding was lower in the ecstasy group throughout the cerebral cortex and in the hippocampus (region-by-group interaction F(12,1152)=7.24, p corrected <0.0001; regional p corrected <0.001), with the occipital cortex most affected (-46%), and was unchanged in caudate, putamen, ventral striatum, globus pallidus, thalamus and midbrain.
key_findings.locator: Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 2nd paragraph; Figure 1

key_findings.finding: After partial-volume correction the reductions were of similar size: occipital -39%, temporal -34%, hippocampus -31%, cingulate -30%, insular -27%, parietal -19%, frontal -17% (p<0.01).
key_findings.note: The parietal and hippocampal figures are printed without a minus sign although described as decreases. The abstract's range (-19% to -46%) mixes partial-volume-corrected and uncorrected values; the uncorrected regional values are not printed in the text.

key_findings.finding: Three kinetic models gave the same answer (occipital -46%, -46%, -41%; hippocampus -21%, -21%, -15%; striatum +3%, +2%, +8%), and the voxel-wise analysis found its largest cluster in occipital cortex with a peak magnitude of -62%.
key_findings.locator: Results, same section, last paragraph; Results, 'Voxel-wise analysis'; Figure 2

key_findings.finding: Individual values overlapped between groups in most regions; in the insular cortex 51% of the ecstasy group fell below the lowest control value. Effect sizes for binding were 1.14 (occipital) and 1.10 (insular).
key_findings.locator: Results, 'PET [11C]DASB non-displaceable binding potential', 4th paragraph (p. 1787, overlap); Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes…' (p. 1792, the 51% figure, also in the Abstract on p. 1779); Discussion, cognitive section (p. 1793, effect sizes)

key_findings.finding: Within the ecstasy group, only years of use and maximum dose predicted lower cortical binding (F(2,44)=9.57, p<0.0001); years of use also predicted lower caudate binding (F(1,41)=4.91, p=0.032). There was no relation between days since last use and binding, with abstinence typically 1-2 months.
Reductions were of similar size in men and women (occipital -51% vs -40%; insular -22% vs -31%; hippocampus -21% in both), unlike the sex difference reported from SPECT.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 'Preferential SERT changes occurred in cerebral cortex and hippocampus'

key_findings.finding: The reduction held in subgroups defined by hair-confirmed methamphetamine (interaction F(12,1140)=4.28, p=0.002) and cocaine, by cannabis, ketamine, LSD, mushrooms and smoking, and was unrelated to sex, body mass index, Axis I diagnosis, hormone levels or serotonin-transporter genotype.

Brain structure did not explain the finding: no group difference in whole-brain, ventricular, white-matter, cortical or subcortical volumes; cortical thinning in the ecstasy group was mostly accounted for by co-use of methamphetamine and, in the rest, by IQ; thickness and volume were unrelated to binding (p>0.05).

The ecstasy group scored lower on verbal memory (CVLT group F(1,93)=8.53, p=0.004; short-delay free recall -17.8%), working memory (PASAT, Digit Ordering), Trails B and Symbol Digit, with effect sizes 0.43-0.86 after adjustment for education or verbal IQ, but not on the Denman or Warrington memory tests; scores of both groups were in the normal range.
key_findings.locator: Table 4 (p. 1790); Results, 'Neuropsychological testing' (pp. 1789-1790); Discussion, cognitive section (p. 1793, the effect-size range)
key_findings.note: Cognitive tests were run one-tailed because only deficits were of interest (p. 1783).

key_findings.finding: Lower insular and hippocampal binding went with poorer short-delay verbal recall (rho=0.38, p=0.004) and slower Trails B (rho=-0.38 and -0.35), uncorrected for multiplicity.

Hair toxicology showed MDMA in all 49 participants, MDA in 82%, methamphetamine or amphetamine in 65% and cocaine in 47%; only 9 of 32 people with methamphetamine-positive hair reported recent use (p=0.016).
key_findings.locator: Results, 'Demographic characteristics and drug profiles', 2nd paragraph (p. 1784); Table 2 (p. 1785)

reporting_issues.issue: The length of hair tested is given in the Results as 2.3 inches in men and 10.5 inches in women (about 5 and 21 months) and in the Discussion as 2.6 and 10.3 inches (5 and 20 months).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the hair window is the basis for the claim that recent methamphetamine use does not explain the finding; the two figures should agree.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives the cortical range as -19% to -46% and the hippocampus as -21%, while the Results list partial-volume-corrected values of -17% to -39% with a hippocampal value of -31%; the uncorrected regional values other than occipital (-46%) and hippocampus (-21%) are not printed.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader cannot reconstruct the abstract's range from the printed numbers, and later sources quote the two sets interchangeably (the 2016 review lists the corrected values as the study's result).

reporting_issues.issue: Partial-volume-corrected decreases are printed as 'parietal, 19%' and 'hippocampus, 31%' without minus signs in a list where the other values carry them.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographic only; the direction is given in the sentence.

reporting_issues.issue: Subcortical grey-matter volumes were below normal in the 17 people whose hair was negative for methamphetamine but normal in those whose hair was positive.
reporting_issues.consequence: The paper calls this apparently paradoxical and explains it by above-normal striatal volume reported in people who use methamphetamine; it shows that the subgroup comparisons are not straightforward to interpret.

reporting_issues.issue: Cognitive comparisons used one-tailed tests, chosen because only deficits were of interest, and the correlations between binding and cognition are reported without correction for multiplicity.
reporting_issues.consequence: The cognitive p-values are half the two-tailed values, and the binding-cognition correlations (rho about 0.35-0.38) are the weakest part of the paper; the Discussion does not rest its conclusions on them.

verification.source_read: PDF, pp. 1779-1797 (all pages; Tables 1-4 and the text read in the extraction, Figure 1 checked on the rendered page 1786; supplementary tables and figures not read)
